content: The Proterozoic Eon is a geological time period that predates the emergence of abundant complex life on Earth. It spans from approximately 2.5 billion years ago to 541 million years ago and represents the most recent part of the informal Precambrian time. This eon is divided into three distinct geological eras, listed from oldest to youngest: the Paleoproterozoic, the Mesoproterozoic, and the Neoproterozoic. Key events during the Proterozoic include the transition to an oxygen-rich atmosphere during the Mesoproterozoic, several glaciations (notably the hypothesized Snowball Earth during the Cryogenian period in the late Neoproterozoic), and the Ediacaran Period (635 to 541 million years ago), which is marked by the evolution of abundant soft-bodied multicellular organisms. The geological record of the Proterozoic is significantly more complete than that of the preceding Archean Eon. Unlike the deep-water deposits characteristic of the Archean, the Proterozoic features extensive shallow epicontinental seas, with many of the associated rock strata being less metamorphosed or even unaltered. These rocks provide evidence of massive and rapid continental accretion, supercontinent cycles, and modern-style orogenic (mountain-building) activity unique to this eon. The first known glaciations occurred during the Proterozoic, with one beginning shortly after the eon’s onset and at least four during the Neoproterozoic, culminating in the Snowball Earth event associated with the Varangian glaciation. One of the most significant events of the Proterozoic was the accumulation of oxygen in Earth's atmosphere. Around 3 billion years ago, atmospheric oxygen levels were likely only 1–2% of their current levels. By approximately 2 billion years ago, red beds (rocks colored by hematite) began to appear, indicating a rise in atmospheric oxygen. This oxygen build-up is thought to have resulted from the saturation of chemical sinks and an increase in carbon burial, which sequestered organic compounds that would otherwise have been oxidized by the atmosphere. The Proterozoic also saw significant paleogeographic developments. For example, the Mackenzie dike swarm in Canada’s Canadian Shield is the largest known dike swarm on Earth and was a source of massive flood basalt eruptions throughout the eon. This dike swarm is believed to have originated from a mantle plume center known as the Mackenzie hotspot. Life during the Proterozoic underwent critical advancements. The first complex single-celled and multicellular organisms emerged, coinciding with the accumulation of free oxygen in the atmosphere. This may have been driven by an increase in oxidized nitrates, which eukaryotes utilize, in contrast to cyanobacteria. The Proterozoic also marked the evolution of the first symbiotic relationships between mitochondria (present in nearly all eukaryotes) and chloroplasts (found in plants and some protists) with their host cells, approximately 2 billion years ago. Traditionally, the boundary between the Proterozoic and the Phanerozoic eons was defined at the base of the Cambrian Period, marked by the first appearance of animal fossils such as trilobites and archaeocyathids. However, in the latter half of the 20th century, numerous fossil forms were discovered in Proterozoic rocks. Despite these findings, the upper boundary of the Proterozoic remains fixed at the base of the Cambrian, currently dated to 541 million years ago.
